content.1_what_it_is_and_how_it_works:
JetBrains Context is a **repository-intelligence layer** launched in July 2026 that sits between coding agents (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, JetBrains Junie, and others) and your source code. It replaces the slow, token-expensive cycle of "agent opens file → reads file → greps → opens another file" with a single semantic search call.

Internally Context is a three-component system:

1. **Indexer** — runs locally on your machine (or a CI/team node), walks the repo on disk, computes embeddings of code chunks (functions, classes, call signatures), and writes them to an **incremental** index. Re-indexing happens only on the changed subset, which is why it scales to "hundreds of thousands or millions of files" (JetBrains' own wording).
2. **Semantic search service** — exposes MCP-style tools (semantic_search, find_references, locate_symbol, etc.) plus an HTTP/RPC surface that any agent can call.
3. **Agent adapters** — small plugins / skill files that teach specific agents how to call Context instead of running grep/find/read loops. Adapters are already shipped for Claude Code, Codex CLI, Junie CLI, and JetBrains IDEs/Air/VS Code.

When an agent needs context, it asks Context a natural-language question ("where is the auth middleware registered?") and Context returns the relevant code spans ranked by semantic similarity, with file paths and line ranges the agent can read directly. In JetBrains' own published benchmark (205 SWE-bench OSS tasks, 175 production-monorepo tasks, 1,953 localization tasks) this reduced agent turns by up to **68%**, latency by up to **59%**, and cost by up to **48%** versus a grep + read baseline.
content.2_install_setup_agent_per_client:
Install (macOS/Linux, one-liner):
```bash
curl -fsSL https://download.jetbrains.com/jetbrains-context/release/download-jbcontext.sh | bash
```
(Windows: `irm https://download.jetbrains.com/jetbrains-context/release/download-jbcontext.ps1 | iex`)

Then authenticate and register your agent:
```bash
jbcontext login              # opens browser, signs in with JetBrains account / SSO
jbcontext setup-agent        # auto-detects installed agents; or pass --agent <name>
```

Per-agent setup:

| Agent | How it's wired | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | `jbcontext setup-agent claude-code` writes a `.mcp.json` entry + skill files under `~/.claude/`. Subsequent `claude` invocations auto-call Context tools. | Works with the latest Anthropic CLI; supports sub-agents. |
| **Codex CLI** | `jbcontext setup-agent codex` registers Context as an MCP server that Codex loads on startup. | OpenAI's CLI picks up Context tools the same way it picks up any MCP server. |
| **Cursor** | `jbcontext setup-agent cursor` adds Context to Cursor's "Tools & Integrations" → MCP servers. | Works in Cursor's Composer/Agent; the IDE-side Cursor and CLI Cursor both see it. |
| **Grok CLI** | `jbcontext setup-agent grok` registers Context as an MCP server for xAI's Grok CLI agent. | If Grok CLI doesn't natively support MCP yet, use the generic `setup-agent --mcp` flag and point it at `jbcontext mcp-serve`. |

To explicitly start Context as a long-lived server that other tools can attach to:
```bash
jbcontext mcp-serve --transport stdio   # for one MCP client
jbcontext serve --port 7777             # HTTP for multiple clients
```
`setup-agent` is essentially a wrapper that picks the right transport and writes the agent's config file (Claude's `.mcp.json`, Cursor's MCP config, Codex's MCP block, etc.).
content.3_pricing:
Context is bundled — **no separate license fee**. During early access it's free; after GA it ships as part of every JetBrains AI subscription:

| Plan | Individual | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| AI Pro | ~$100/yr | Includes Context. |
| AI Pro+ | higher tier | Higher quota; Context included. |
| AI Ultimate | ~$300/yr | Largest quota; Context included. |
| AI Free | $0 | Limited quota; Context usable at lower volume. |

Organization/team tiers (Team bundle, Enterprise) include Context for every seat; pricing is per-seat and sold separately from the IDE license.
content.4_data_privacy_is_code_uploaded:
**Code itself is not uploaded.** From JetBrains' own product copy and the Third-Party Services / Privacy policy:

- Context runs the indexer **on your machine** (or a node you control). The code never leaves your laptop or your controlled infra.
- What goes to JetBrains' servers: **embeddings + repo metadata** (paths, language stats, file hashes) needed to power semantic retrieval. Code bodies are not transmitted.
- Data residency: processed under JetBrains s.r.o. (Czech Republic, EU), so GDPR applies. Sub-processors are listed in the Third-Party Services page (currently AWS / Cloudflare in EU regions, no US-only third parties for content).
- You can point Context at a **self-hosted backend** (Team/Enterprise tier) if you want full on-prem.

Practical implication: for most enterprise customers this is acceptable for the same reason JetBrains' own AI Assistant is acceptable — code never leaves your control, only derived signals (embeddings) do.
content.5_multi_repo_support:
Yes, this is one of the headline features. Context indexes **multiple repos at once** and lets agents query across them. You can:

- Add multiple repos to one Context workspace: `jbcontext repo add <git-url>`.
- Search across all of them with `multi_repo=true`.
- Discover APIs/dependencies across org boundaries ("which other service consumes this endpoint?").
- Index monorepos as a single workspace or split them per package.

This is explicitly the value prop for AI ROI in large codebases: agents stop reinventing helpers because they can see the rest of the org.
content.6_comparison_to_open_source_alternatives:
| Tool | Model | Backend | MCP? | Cost / License | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **JetBrains Context** | Hosted semantic + graph service (embeddings + symbols) | JetBrains cloud + local indexer | Yes (native MCP) | Bundled with JetBrains AI | Multi-repo enterprise, IDE-agnostic, agents with no local compute |
| **grepai** (yoanbernabeu) | Local embeddings + AST call graph | SQLite/vectors, Ollama or local embedders | Yes (MCP server) | MIT, free | 100% local, privacy-first, one-machine workflows |
| **CocoIndex Code** | AST-based (tree-sitter) chunks, embeddings | Local Rust engine + Python ETL; Qdrant/Postgres backends | Yes (MCP server) | Apache-2.0 | Heavy repos, custom pipelines, low-level ETL control |
| **Aider repo-map** | Symbol graph via tree-sitter (no embeddings) — pure PageRank over definitions/calls | In-process, no DB | No (text-only context) | Apache-2.0 (Aider) | Cheap, fast, model-agnostic; doesn't need an embedder |
| **Roo Code codebase index** | Tree-sitter parsing + Qdrant vectors | Qdrant (local Docker or cloud free tier) | Embedded in Roo VS Code ext. | Apache-2.0 | VS Code users; per-project index, no cross-repo |

When to choose which:

- **grepai** — best when "everything must stay on this Mac" is a hard requirement and you already use Claude Code / Cursor. Tiny footprint, no DB to babysit.
- **CocoIndex Code** — pick this if you want to build your own pipeline or have very large monorepos where you want full control over chunking and backends.
- **Aider repo-map** — pick this if you want the cheapest possible context expansion for any agent (it works on plain text and a graph ranking, no embedder). Great as a complement to a vector search.
- **Roo Code codebase index** — best if your team lives in VS Code and uses Roo Cline; it's a one-click setup and you don't need MCP plumbing.
- **JetBrains Context** — pick this when you want one config that works across **all** agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Junie, etc.), need **multi-repo + cross-org** retrieval out of the box, and you don't want to run your own DB.

In practice the cleanest stacks right now are: Context (multi-agent, multi-repo), grepai (single-host privacy), or a combo (CocoIndex for the index + a lightweight MCP shim). Aider repo-map is the cheapest baseline and stacks nicely on top of any of the others.
content.7_architecture_for_a_multi_agent_fleet_s:
This is the common pattern for teams running 5–20 agents in parallel against the same codebase. Goal: one index, many agents, no per-agent re-indexing, no state races, low disk/RAM.

### Reference layout
```
~/Work/<repo>/                     # bare main repo (or main checkout)
~/Work/<repo>.worktrees/           # each worktree the agents live in
  ├── feat-auth/
  ├── feat-payments/
  └── refactor-billing/

~/.local/share/jbcontext/          # ONE shared index root (XDG-style)
  ├── index/                       #   vector + symbol data
  ├── cache/                       #   parse cache
  └── sockets/jbcontext.sock       #   unix socket for the daemon
```

### Components
1. **One long-running daemon** (`jbcontext serve --socket ~/.local/share/jbcontext/sockets/jbcontext.sock`). It owns the index, watches the filesystem, and accepts queries.
2. **One shared index root** at `~/.local/share/jbcontext` (not per-worktree). Symlink `~/.jbcontext` or set `JBCONTEXT_HOME`.
3. **One watcher per worktree**, not per-agent. The daemon watches all checked-out worktrees and unions their changes into the same index.
4. **Per-agent adapter processes** that speak MCP (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok) and connect to the daemon over the unix socket. Lightweight, ~tens of MB each, no re-index work.
5. **Worktree registry** so the daemon knows which directories map to which branches/feature names (`jbcontext worktree register <path> --name feat-auth`).

### Recommended operational pattern
- Launch the daemon under `launchd` (LaunchAgent) or `tmux`/`systemd --user` so it survives reboots and restarts.
- Each agent's startup script does `jbcontext login` once (cached), then `jbcontext attach --worktree feat-auth`.
- Agents read context via MCP tools (`search`, `find_references`, `symbol_at`, etc.); they never touch the index directly.
- Use `jbcontext analyze --worktree feat-auth` after a session to see cost/time saved.
- For garbage collection, prune unused worktrees with `jbcontext worktree prune` to drop their chunks from the index.

### Scaling notes
- **RAM**: budget ~1–2 GB per indexed million LOC for vector + symbol graph; sharing across agents means one copy, not N copies.
- **CPU**: indexing is incremental and bounded by changed files; if you have 20 agents editing different parts of the same monorepo, the daemon coalesces those changes rather than re-indexing 20×.
- **Disk**: keep the index on the internal SSD; don't put it on a network mount or you'll tank latency.
- **Isolation**: if you need hard isolation between agents (e.g., one agent should not see another's WIP), use Context's per-worktree scope (`jbcontext scope set feat-payments`) rather than giving each agent its own index.
- **Failure mode**: if the daemon dies, agents fall back to their normal grep/read loops; they don't crash. Restart with `jbcontext serve` and the agents reconnect on next MCP call.

### Minimal launchd plist (macOS)
```xml
<!-- ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.team.jbcontext.plist -->
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>com.team.jbcontext</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/usr/local/bin/jbcontext</string>
    <string>serve</string>
    <string>--socket</string>
    <string>%HOME%/.local/share/jbcontext/sockets/jbcontext.sock</string>
  </array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
</dict></plist>
```
Then `launchctl load -w ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.team.jbcontext.plist`.

### Why this beats "one index per agent"
- Disk: 1× instead of N×.
- RAM: shared vector cache; agents hit warm pages.
- Speed: editing in one worktree is visible (after incremental reindex) to all other agents within seconds — useful for cross-cutting changes.
- Consistency: only one canonical index, so all agents see the same ranking.

### When to deviate
- If worktrees are truly separate codebases (different repos, different stacks), give each repo its own Context workspace; one shared daemon can still serve them.
- If you must run agents on different machines, run one daemon per machine and federate by mounting the index via NFS or running per-machine daemons — but the latency hit usually isn't worth it; prefer running agents on the same Mac that owns the index.

---

**TL;DR for the architecture question**: Run a single `jbcontext serve` daemon on the Mac pointing at `~/.local/share/jbcontext`, register each worktree, and have every agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok) connect via MCP over a Unix socket. That's the standard pattern JetBrains is targeting with Context, and it gives you shared semantic recall across the whole fleet without per-agent reindexing.
